# Opportunity map

**Status: draft for the author's review.** The ratings below are judgment, not measurement, and the author is
expected to change them. No market statistics are used.

Where could a language-model tool help a bank's investment and lending teams? Each workflow is rated on three
things:

- **Value**: time saved and decisions improved if the tool works.
- **Feasibility**: whether the data can be reached and the output checked against a source, with public tools.
- **Risk**: the harm if an error goes unnoticed (High is worse).

| Workflow | Value | Feasibility | Risk | One-line reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Credit memo drafting | High | High | Medium | Much of a review is assembling figures and filing text, which XBRL and filings provide in checkable form; errors reach a credit committee, so every figure must be traceable. |
| Financial spreading | High | Medium | Medium | Entering statements into the bank's template is repetitive; public filers have XBRL, but private borrowers send PDFs. |
| Covenant extraction and monitoring | High | Low | High | Covenants sit in long credit agreements with bespoke definitions, and a missed breach is costly. |
| Portfolio surveillance of filings | Medium | High | Low | New filings are easy to detect and ratios are deterministic; flags only prompt a human to look. |
| New-issue document summaries | Medium | Medium | Medium | Offering documents are long and often private; summaries help triage but need careful citation. |
| Committee reporting packs | Medium | Medium | Medium | Assembling packs is routine, but the inputs are internal data a public prototype cannot reach. |
| Peer comparison screens | Medium | High | Low | Ratios across peers come straight from XBRL; the judgment stays with the analyst. |
| Earnings call and news monitoring | Medium | High | Medium | Text is plentiful, but sources vary in reliability and timing. |
| Onboarding document checks | Medium | Medium | High | Document checks are repetitive, but mistakes have regulatory consequences. |

## Why credit memo drafting

- It joins structured data (XBRL facts, which can be checked exactly) with narrative (which must be grounded
  in quoted passages), so it exercises the whole control story: computed figures, quoted figures, an
  independent judge and a human sign-off.
- It needs only public data (SEC EDGAR), so the prototype handles no confidential information.
- Banks already have a human review step for memos (the analyst and the credit committee), so the tool fits an
  existing control rather than inventing one.
- Portfolio surveillance came along cheaply, because it reuses the same ratio engine with no model at all.

## What would change the ratings

Access to a bank's own data (private borrowers' statements, credit agreements, internal ratings) would raise
the feasibility of spreading, covenant monitoring and committee packs. Evidence from the timing log
(02-effort-comparison.md) would replace the value judgments with measured effort for the memo workflow.

# Manual against tool-assisted effort

Does the tool save time without adding errors? This document holds the protocol, the log template and the
results. Every result comes from timings the author records in `evals/timings.csv`; none is estimated.

## Results

No timings recorded yet: every effort figure is pending (n = 0).

"Errors found later" counts mistakes discovered afterwards, when the memo is checked against the author's
hand-verified golden sheet.

## Protocol

1. **Tasks.** (a) Write the six-section memo for one company from its latest 10-K and 10-Q. (b) Answer the five
   golden fact questions for one company.
2. **Conditions.** *Manual*: filings, a calculator and a blank memo outline only. *Tool-assisted*: start from
   Sourcebound's memo, work through the reviewer checklist, correct or remove anything wrong, and sign off.
3. **Companies.** Use a company in only one condition, so that knowing its filings from the first attempt does
   not speed up the second. Alternate which condition comes first from one company to the next.
4. **Timing.** Start when the first filing (or the memo) is opened; stop when the memo is complete (manual) or
   signed off (tool-assisted). Record whole minutes; note interruptions.
5. **Errors found later.** After both conditions, check each memo's figures and facts against the golden sheet
   and record the number of mistakes.
6. **Honesty.** Record every attempt, including abandoned or slow ones, with a note. Never round towards the
   expected answer.

## Log template

One row per timed task, in `evals/timings.csv`:

```
date,company,condition,task,start,end,minutes,errors found later,notes
```

`condition` is `manual` or `tool-assisted`; `task` is `memo` or `fact questions`.

## Limits of this comparison

One person (the author) does every task, so the results describe one analyst, not a team. Samples are small and
learning effects remain despite the counterbalancing. The comparison measures drafting and checking time only,
not the committee's review.

# Model recommendation

**Status: provisional.** The figures that decide the choice (human labels and judge calibration) are pending
until the author labels the claim sample, so this memo sets out what has been measured and the rule for
choosing, not the final choice.

Source of every figure: `evals/results/results.json`, generated 2026-11-18 07:51 UTC by
`uv run python -m sourcebound.evals.report` from the saved model outputs. Costs are at Sail list prices
read on 2026-11-17. Each rate shows its sample size (n).

## Writers: accuracy, latency and cost per memo

| Measure | DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 | DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 | GLM-5.3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model ID | deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 | deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 | zai-org/GLM-5.3 |
| Memos drafted (first run) | 15 | 15 | 15 |
| Claims per memo | 32.7 | 34.0 | 35.1 |
| Judge: supported | 92.3% (n = 491) | 91.6% (n = 510) | 85.9% (n = 526) |
| Judge: partly supported | 7.1% (n = 491) | 8.0% (n = 510) | 13.5% (n = 526) |
| Judge: unsupported | 0.6% (n = 491) | 0.4% (n = 510) | 0.6% (n = 526) |
| Quoted figures found in the cited passage | 100.0% (n = 75) | 100.0% (n = 23) | 100.0% (n = 65) |
| Engine figures matching hand-checked values | pending (n = 0) | pending (n = 0) | pending (n = 0) |
| Unsupported-claim rate (human labels) | pending (n = 0) | pending (n = 0) | pending (n = 0) |
| Citation precision (human labels) | pending (n = 0) | pending (n = 0) | pending (n = 0) |
| Raw numbers rejected per memo | 3.1 | 1.2 | 2.3 |
| Repairs per memo | 1.6 | 1.3 | 2.1 |
| Cost per memo (USD, list price) | $0.178 | $0.030 | $0.107 |
| Model time per memo | 1365 s | 476 s | 251 s |
| Run-to-run: judge supported | 91.4% (89.3% to 94.6%, 3 runs) | 87.7% (87.1% to 88.3%, 3 runs) | 80.9% (77.8% to 83.4%, 3 runs) |

What the rows mean:

- *Judge: supported / partly / unsupported*: the share of all drafted claims each verdict was given, by the
  provisional judge (GLM-5.3). GLM-5.3 also judged its own writing here, which may favour it.
- *Quoted figures found in the cited passage*: figures the model copied from filing text, checked by code.
- *Engine figures matching hand-checked values* and the two *human labels* rows: pending until the author's golden
  sheets and claim labels are entered.
- *Raw numbers rejected*: figures the writer typed instead of using a placeholder, caught by code before
  publication.
- *Model time*: the sum of the model calls' latencies for one memo.
- *Run-to-run*: the golden five companies drafted three times, to show how much results vary between runs.

## Judges: agreement with human labels

| Judge | Claims judged | Agreement with human labels | False-pass rate | Cost (USD) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 | 180 | pending (n = 0) | pending (n = 0) | $0.4128 |
| zai-org/GLM-5.3 | 180 | pending (n = 0) | pending (n = 0) | $0.1248 |

The false-pass rate is the dangerous error: of the claims the author labels unsupported, the share the judge
called supported.

## Seeded errors: which check catches what

| Judge | Error planted | n | Caught by code | Judge: unsupported | Judge: partly | Missed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 | negation | 60 | 0 of 60 | 57 of 60 | 0 of 60 | 3 of 60 |
| deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 | citation swap | 43 | 43 of 43 | 0 of 43 | 0 of 43 | 0 of 43 |
| deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 | citation swap with quote | 43 | 7 of 43 | 27 of 43 | 6 of 43 | 3 of 43 |
| deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 | raw number | 24 | 24 of 24 | 0 of 24 | 0 of 24 | 0 of 24 |
| deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 | wrong placeholder | 22 | 0 of 22 | 5 of 22 | 17 of 22 | 0 of 22 |
| zai-org/GLM-5.3 | negation | 60 | 0 of 60 | 54 of 60 | 4 of 60 | 2 of 60 |
| zai-org/GLM-5.3 | citation swap | 43 | 43 of 43 | 0 of 43 | 0 of 43 | 0 of 43 |
| zai-org/GLM-5.3 | citation swap with quote | 43 | 7 of 43 | 26 of 43 | 7 of 43 | 3 of 43 |
| zai-org/GLM-5.3 | raw number | 24 | 24 of 24 | 0 of 24 | 0 of 24 | 0 of 24 |
| zai-org/GLM-5.3 | wrong placeholder | 22 | 0 of 22 | 8 of 22 | 11 of 22 | 3 of 22 |

By design, typed figures and citations moved without their quote are caught by code; negations, swapped
placeholders and citations moved together with a real quote depend on the judge. The table shows how that
worked in practice.

## Rule for choosing (proposed before the labels are in)

1. **Judge first.** Choose the candidate with the lower false-pass rate on the labelled sample; if they are
   close, prefer the higher agreement, then the lower cost.
2. **Then the writer.** Re-judge every writer's claims with the chosen judge (from the saved drafts, no new
   drafting). Drop any writer whose human-labelled unsupported-claim rate is clearly worse than the best, given
   the sample sizes. Among the rest, prefer lower cost per memo, then lower model time.
3. **Record the choice** in the decision log with the figures and their sample sizes, and update this memo.

Until then, GLM-5.3 is the provisional writer and judge (a setting chosen in phase 4, not a result).

# Risk and control table

Each way Sourcebound can fail, the control that catches it, the evidence that the control works, and the
matching term from the 2026 interagency model-risk guidance.

## Scope: what this table borrows, and what it does not claim

- The Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC issued revised "Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management" on
  17 April 2026 (Fed SR 26-2, OCC Bulletin 2026-13, FDIC FIL-15-2026). For the Federal Reserve it replaces
  SR 11-7 (2011); the OCC and FDIC rescinded their own earlier versions.
- **This table borrows the guidance's vocabulary by choice.** It does not claim that the guidance applies to this
  project or that the project complies with it:
  - The guidance's "model" is a complex quantitative method applying statistical, economic or financial theory,
    and it "excludes simple arithmetic calculations ... as well as deterministic rule-based processes". The ratio
    engine is deterministic arithmetic, so it is not a model under this definition.
  - Its footnote 3 says generative AI and agentic AI models "are not within the scope of this guidance", and that
    a banking organization's own risk management and governance practices should determine controls for tools
    it does not cover. The writer, the judge and the follow-up loop are generative AI, so they are outside it.
  - It is expected to be most relevant to banking organizations with over $30 billion in total assets, and it
    "does not set forth enforceable standards or prescriptive requirements".
- For context only: OCC Bulletin 2026-54 (4 November 2026) gives OCC examiners a framework for banks' use of
  what it calls super intelligence, and states that it "does not establish supervisory expectations for banks".
  Its illustrative risk tiers list "internal document summarization for credit memos" in a moderate tier with
  mandatory human-in-the-loop review, which is how this tool is designed to be used.
- Sail (the model provider) is a third party. The interagency third-party risk-management guidance of June 2023
  (SR 23-4, OCC Bulletin 2023-17, FIL-29-2023) describes a life cycle of planning, due diligence and selection,
  contract negotiation, ongoing monitoring and termination. A replacement was proposed in September 2026 and is
  open for comment until 16 December 2026.

Evidence figures come from `evals/results/results.json` (generated 2026-11-18 07:51 UTC), using the
provisional judge, zai-org/GLM-5.3. "Pending" figures need the author's golden values or claim labels.

## The table

| Failure mode | Control | Evidence it works | Guidance term (borrowed) |
|---|---|---|---|
| The engine picks the wrong XBRL fact (wrong tag, period or restated value) | Ranked fallback chains in config; period and year-to-date alignment checks; most recently filed value with restatements logged; fallbacks listed on the reviewer checklist | tests/test_resolver.py, tests/test_periods.py, tests/test_concepts_config.py; engine figures against hand-checked golden values: pending (n = 0) | Model testing; documentation (the engine itself is not a model under the definition) |
| A missing figure is filled in with a guess | A missing fact is "not available", never estimated; it goes on the checklist | tests/test_ratios.py (`test_missing_input_is_not_available`), tests/test_periods.py (`test_missing_prior_year_is_reported_not_guessed`) | Model use: limitations |
| The writer types a wrong number | Engine figures are placeholders filled by code; any typed figure must appear in a cited passage | tests/test_number_and_quote_checks.py; raw numbers rejected per GLM-5.3 memo: 2.3; seeded typed figures caught by code: 24 of 24 | Model development: conceptual soundness of the design; model testing |
| A quote is not in the passage it cites, or cites a passage the model never saw | Quote check against the cited passage; citations limited to passages shown | tests/test_number_and_quote_checks.py; seeded citations moved without their quote, caught by code: 43 of 43; GLM-5.3 quoted figures found in the cited passage: 100.0% (n = 65) | Outcomes analysis |
| A claim overstates or contradicts its evidence | An independent judge reads each claim with its passages and metric values; partly supported and unsupported claims are marked and listed for review | Seeded negations judged unsupported: 54 of 60; human-labelled unsupported-claim rate (GLM-5.3 writer): pending (n = 0) | Outcomes analysis; effective challenge |
| The judge passes an unsupported claim | Judge calibrated against a blind human-labelled sample; the judge is chosen by its false-pass rate; the reviewer checklist | GLM-5.3 false-pass rate: pending (n = 0); agreement with labels: pending (n = 0) | Effective challenge; model validation |
| Writer and judge share a blind spot | Two judge candidates calibrated separately; seeded errors run through each | Seeded swapped placeholders missed by the GLM-5.3 judge: 3 of 22; by the DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 judge: 0 of 22 | Aggregate risk |
| Results change from run to run | Fixed six-section pipeline; every request and response saved; run-to-run spread measured | GLM-5.3 share of claims judged supported across three runs: 80.9% (77.8% to 83.4%, 3 runs) | Ongoing model monitoring |
| A memo goes stale after a new filing | Daily job detects new filings, recomputes ratios and flags, and marks the memo stale until it is regenerated and reviewed | tests/test_watchlist.py (`test_new_filing_refreshes_flags_and_marks_the_memo_stale`); reports/watchlist-simulation.md | Ongoing model monitoring; model use |
| Output is used beyond its purpose (the SB grade read as a credit rating, or investment advice) | Disclaimer on every page; SB grades named as a stylized scorecard; the follow-up box refuses out-of-scope questions | tests/test_api.py (`test_out_of_scope_passes_through`); tests/test_scorecard.py (the scorecard never reads agency ratings) | Model use: intended purpose and limitations; statement of purpose |
| Unreviewed model text is published | The daily job makes no model call; memos are regenerated and reviewed by hand; live answers keep only supported claims and list the rest | tests/test_watchlist.py (`test_watchlist_code_imports_no_model_client`); tests/test_api.py (`test_claims_that_fail_verification_are_removed_with_the_reason`) | Governance and controls: roles and responsibilities |
| The provider changes, reprices or retires a model, or goes down | Model IDs and prices pinned in config with the date read; idempotent retries; plain "busy" and "unavailable" errors; saved outputs allow re-judging without new drafting | tests/test_llm_provider.py (`test_retries_reuse_the_same_idempotency_key`); tests/test_api.py (`test_provider_errors_map_to_plain_http_errors`); tests/test_replay.py | Vendor and other third-party products; third-party ongoing monitoring and termination |
| The API key leaks | Key only in .env and server environment variables; never printed or sent to the browser | tests/test_llm_provider.py (`test_settings_never_show_the_key`, `test_bad_request_is_not_retried_and_never_leaks_the_key`); a check of the built site before deploy | Governance and controls |
| Someone runs up the model bill through the public question box | Question length cap, bounded lookups, capped output tokens; a per-IP rate limit before production | tests/test_api.py (`test_bad_requests_get_400_with_a_plain_message`, `test_tool_loop_stops_after_three_rounds_then_asks_for_the_answer_without_tools`) | Governance and controls |
| Nobody can tell which model, prompt or data produced a memo | Each memo records its writer, judge, settings, price date, filings used and raw-output file; the decision log records every design choice | tests/test_published_contract.py (every published file matches its contract); docs/strategy/06-decision-log.md | Model inventory; documentation |

## What is missing

Pending figures need the author's golden values and claim labels. In a bank, the human sign-off would be recorded
on a server with the reviewer's name and time; here it stays in one browser. An independent validator, who
provides effective challenge, is part of the rollout plan, not of this prototype.

documents.markdown:
<!-- Generated from docs/strategy/templates/05-rollout-plan.md by `uv run python -m sourcebound.pipeline.build_strategy`. Edit the template, not this file. -->

# Rollout plan

How a bank could introduce a tool like Sourcebound safely. Thresholds are left for the model owner to set from
the calibration results; none is invented here.

## Stages

1. **Shadow.** A small pilot group writes memos as usual. The tool drafts the same memos in parallel, and the
   two are compared. Nothing from the tool reaches a credit committee.
2. **Assisted.** The tool's memo becomes the analyst's first draft. The analyst must work through the reviewer
   checklist and sign off; the memo the committee sees is the analyst's, with every figure still linked to its
   source.
3. **Wider use.** Extend sector by sector, starting with US public companies that file XBRL, the population the
   tool was tested on.

Each stage continues only if the monitoring below stays inside the limits set before the stage began.

## Pilot group

A few credit analysts and one reviewer, covering one sector of public borrowers, plus an independent
validator who did not build the tool and who challenges its design and results (effective challenge).

## The human review step

- Every unsupported or partly supported claim is fixed or removed before sign-off.
- Every checklist item (figure not available, fallback tag, blank taken as zero, stale data) is ticked by a named
  reviewer. In a bank, sign-off is recorded on a server with the reviewer's name, the time and the memo version;
  this prototype keeps it in one browser only.
- A second reviewer samples signed-off memos each month and labels their claims, which keeps the judge's error
  rate measured.

## What gets logged

- Every model request and response, with the model ID, prompt version, settings and price.
- The verification report for each memo: each figure's source, each claim's verdict and reason.
- The data date and the filings used.
- Checklist sign-offs and what the reviewer changed.
- Follow-up questions, answers and removed claims.
- Errors found after sign-off, with how they were found.

## What would trigger a rollback

- A wrong figure or claim found in a signed-off memo that the checks had marked verified.
- The judge's false-pass rate on the monthly labelled sample rising above the limit set from calibration.
- The share of claims removed or marked unsupported rising above its limit.
- The provider changing or retiring a model, its terms or its prices: re-run the evaluations before resuming.
- A provider outage longer than the business can wait: fall back to the manual process, which stays in place
  throughout the pilot.

Rollback means returning to the previous stage; the manual process is never switched off during the pilot.

documents.title: Decision log
documents.markdown:
# Decision log

Each entry: the decision, why, and the alternatives rejected. Entries D1–D10 are seeded from PLAN.md
section 4.2 (fixed before building started, 17 November 2026). Later entries were made while building and
say which phase made them. Where the plan named no rejected alternative, the entry says so rather than
inventing one.

## Fixed in the plan (PLAN.md 4.2)

### D1. Backend Python 3.12, FastAPI, pandas, pytest; frontend React, Vite, TypeScript
- **Why:** mainstream, readable stacks that the author can explain; Python is the natural home for
  financial data handling and evaluation code; FastAPI runs as a Vercel Python function.
- **Rejected:** none recorded in the plan.

### D2. Inference through Sail Research, behind one interface configured by environment variables
- **Why:** an OpenAI-compatible API giving access to several open-weight models from different labs at
  low list prices, with paid credit already in place. One interface means the model is a config value.
- **Rejected:** the Claude API (the plan fixes Sail as the provider).

### D3. Three writer models: zai-org/GLM-5.3, deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017
- **Why:** two mid-priced models from different labs and one very cheap one, so the recommendation can
  show a cost-against-accuracy trade-off.
- **Rejected:** none recorded in the plan.

### D4. Numbers by placeholder
- **Decision:** the model writes tokens such as `{{m:net_leverage:LTM}}` and code substitutes the value.
- **Why:** a figure the model never types cannot be mistyped; every printed number traces to the engine.
- **Rejected:** letting the model copy numbers from a table, because copying errors are silent.

### D5. The memo is a fixed pipeline, not an agent
- **Why:** the same retrieval steps every time make the memo auditable and repeatable. Only the live
  follow-up endpoint uses a bounded tool loop (two read-only tools, at most three rounds), because
  questions are open-ended.
- **Rejected:** an agentic memo writer that chooses its own lookups (not auditable or repeatable).

### D6. Retrieval: our own BM25 plus routing by filing section; index shipped as JSON files
- **Why:** Sail serves no embedding model; BM25 is small enough to explain line by line and needs no
  second vendor. Retrieval recall is measured in the evals; embeddings are proposed only if measured
  recall is poor.
- **Rejected for now:** local embeddings (large serverless bundle, slow cold starts); a second embedding
  vendor (a second key and provider).

### D7. Hosting: Vercel Hobby, own project, static frontend plus FastAPI as a Python function
- **Why:** free tier, CDN for static JSON, one Python function for the live endpoint. Nothing is held in
  memory between requests; memos, verification reports and the watchlist are generated ahead of time and
  shipped as static JSON with filing dates shown.
- **Rejected:** none recorded in the plan.

### D8. Watchlist refresh: a daily GitHub Actions job with no model call; memo marked stale until regenerated locally and reviewed
- **Why:** the Sail key stays only in Vercel and on the author's laptop, and no memo is published without
  human review, which matches the project's own control story.
- **Rejected:** Vercel Cron (functions cannot write files); automatic memo regeneration (publishes
  unreviewed output).

### D9. Rate limiting: a Vercel Firewall rate-limit rule keyed by IP on /api/ask
- **Why:** no database needed.
- **Rejected:** none recorded in the plan.

### D10. Interface designed separately in Claude Design
- **Decision:** build the data contract first, then a plain placeholder interface, then implement the
  handed-off design in a later phase.
- **Why:** the contract is the stable part; the design can change without touching the engine.
- **Rejected:** none recorded in the plan.

## Made while building

### D11. EDGAR client on httpx with a disk cache that mirrors the URL (phase 1)
- **Why:** httpx has a built-in mock transport, so throttle, retry and cache behaviour is tested with no
  network. Mirroring the URL makes the cache inspectable by hand; a sidecar file records the fetch time,
  which becomes the data date in reports.
- **Rejected:** `requests` (needs an extra mocking library); the standard-library `urllib` (no bundled
  certificates on this machine's Python, and harder to mock).

### D12. Plain dataclasses in the engine instead of pandas for phase 1
- **Why:** a company has a few thousand facts; explicit loops over small dataclasses are easier to walk an
  interviewer through than DataFrame operations. pandas stays in the stack for tabular work where it earns
  its place (coverage reports, evals).
- **Rejected:** loading company facts into a DataFrame.

### D13. Periods anchored on the 10-K's report date and identified by fact dates
- **Why:** the submissions API states the period each filing covers; fact start and end dates are the
  only reliable description of a fact's period.
- **Rejected:** the API's fy/fp fields (they describe the filing, not the fact); the frames API
  (calendar-aligned to within 30 days, which blurs non-calendar fiscal years).

### D14. One tag per LTM value
- **Why:** mixing tags across FY0, current YTD and prior YTD could add numbers with different scopes.
- **Rejected:** falling back window by window.

### D15. Debt reconciliation compares every total-debt candidate, warning above 5%
- **Why:** a tag can cover less than its name suggests. On real data this caught Walmart's rank-1 tag
  omitting short-term borrowings. The check changes no value; it puts the gap in front of the reviewer.
- **Rejected:** trusting rank 1 silently; auto-switching to the larger candidate (that would be a silent
  substitution).

### D16. Phase-1 reports written to reports/ and committed
- **Why:** the hand check needs files that can be diffed across runs. reports/ is not in the plan's
  layout; it holds human-readable check reports, separate from data/published/ (the site's JSON).

### D17. Test fixtures are trimmed captures plus the script that made them
- **Why:** the full responses for three companies are about 13 MB. The capture keeps every chain tag from
  2021 on, unmodified, with the source URL and fetch time; the script makes the trimming reproducible.
- **Rejected:** committing full responses; hand-written fixtures of real companies (not traceable).

### D18. Chain revision 1: finance leases count as debt; components before combined tags (approved 17 November 2026)
- **Decision:** (1) total debt prefers balance-sheet components, adds a candidate pairing
  LongTermDebtAndCapitalLeaseObligations with short-term debt, and moves DebtLongtermAndShorttermCombinedAmount
  to last; (2) finance-lease liabilities count as debt for every company, and finance-lease interest is
  added when only InterestExpenseDebt is reported; (3) capex adds PaymentsToAcquireOtherProductiveAssets
  (Verizon); (4) revenue ranks Revenues (total revenue) first.
- **Why:** the phase-1 tag-discovery and reconciliation reports showed the starting chains understated
  Walmart's debt (the combined tag omits its $6,596m of short-term borrowings at FY0), could not produce
  Verizon's LTM debt or any Verizon capex, and treated finance leases differently by company (inside
  Verizon's and Goodyear's debt lines, separate for Walmart at $6,761m). Finance leases are economically
  borrowings, and credit analysts normally count them as debt.
- **Effect at FY0:** Walmart total debt $38,166m -> $51,523m; Goodyear $5,937m -> $6,198m (its balance-sheet
  total); Verizon unchanged at $158,150m. Verizon's LTM debt ($166,233m) and capex ($17,011m in FY0) became
  available.
- **Consequence for phase 2:** the golden-set template needs a finance-lease row, so a hand-computed total
  debt follows the same definition.
- **Rejected:** debt exactly as each balance sheet presents it (inconsistent across companies); excluding
  finance leases everywhere (needs subtraction from combined tags, and understates debt-like obligations).

### D19. Chain revision 2 (approved 17 November 2026, phase 2)
- **Decision:** net-interest tags (InterestIncomeExpenseNonoperatingNet, InterestIncomeExpenseNet), sign
  flipped and flagged, rank above the cash-interest-paid proxy; amortisation is optional beside
  Depreciation; short-term debt adds LongTermDebtAndCapitalLeaseObligationsCurrent and NotesPayableCurrent,
  and counts as zero when nothing is reported; total debt adds LongTermNotesAndLoans + short-term debt +
  finance leases; the year-1 maturity falls back to the balance-sheet current portion of long-term debt.
- **Why:** the tag-discovery run over all 15 companies showed these were the tags actually used by Union
  Pacific (depreciation only), Kohl's, Cleveland-Cliffs, Community Health and Caesars (net interest), Oracle
  (notes payable), Union Pacific and Community Health (current debt), and HCA (no year-1 maturity tag).
  Afterwards every core ratio is available for every company.
- **Rejected:** keeping the cash-interest-paid proxy (cash paid can differ from expense by timing); leaving
  short-term debt "not available" when untagged (companies usually omit a nil line; the checklist shows each
  assumed zero, so a wrong zero is caught).

### D20. ExxonMobil uses its predecessor registrant (override, approved 17 November 2026)
- **Decision:** config/overrides.yaml maps XOM to Exxon Mobil Corp (CIK 34088) instead of the new holding
  company ExxonMobil Holdings Corp (CIK 2115436), with the written reason; the override is on XOM's checklist.
- **Why:** the new registrant (from 1 July 2026, Form 8-K12B) has no 10-K yet; the predecessor has every
  annual report. Its XBRL data runs to the 10-Q for 31 March 2026 (the June 10-Q's facts sit under the new
  CIK), so XOM's latest figures are about six months older than most companies'.
- **Rejected:** swapping in Occidental; dropping to 14 companies; merging two registrants' facts (more code,
  harder to explain; revisit when the new registrant files its first 10-K).

### D21. One definition of "debt due within 12 months"; ladder metrics as of FY0
- **Decision:** debt due within 12 months is the balance sheet's short-term debt (short-term borrowings plus
  the current portion of long-term debt), used in liquidity coverage and in debt due within 24 months
  (= short-term debt + ladder year 2). Near-term maturity cover divides that by cash + short-term investments
  + undrawn revolver. The ladder metrics are as of FY0, from the 10-K's maturity table.
- **Why:** the balance sheet updates every quarter and includes commercial paper, which the maturity table
  leaves out; one definition everywhere keeps the golden-set formulas and the engine identical.
- **Rejected:** the maturity table's year 1 (omits short-term borrowings; annual only).

### D22. Scorecard rules beyond the plan's grid
- **Decision:** a value exactly on a threshold takes the worse band (approved 17 November 2026). Statuses
  without a value map to fixed bands: EBITDA <= 0 -> 6 on leverage, net leverage and coverage; net cash -> 1;
  no uses of cash -> 1 on liquidity; debt due with no cash or revolver -> 6; zero debt -> 1 on every
  debt-related factor. Interest <= 0 with debt outstanding is not scored. The "latest" grade uses LTM
  ratios and the FY0 near-term maturity cover; an FY0 grade is computed too (for the phase-6 grade-change flag).
- **Why:** the plan's grid notation ("<1.0", "1.0-2.0", ">6.5") leaves exact boundaries ambiguous; a single
  conservative rule is easy to state and test. Fixed bands for special statuses follow the plan's own
  "EBITDA <= 0" and "net cash" entries.
- **Rejected:** "better band" on ties; scoring "not meaningful" as not available (would hide distress).

### D23. Trend direction rule
- **Decision:** direction from FY-2 to LTM; "stable" within 10% of the FY-2 value (and at least 0.1x) for
  multiples, within 2 percentage points for percentages.
- **Why:** a simple, explainable rule that ignores noise. Not tuned on any result.

### D24. Use the newest filing that has facts; flag skipped ones
- **Decision:** the latest 10-K and 10-Q are the newest that have facts in the company's XBRL data; a newer
  filing without facts is skipped and logged as stale data (on the checklist).
- **Why:** facts can lag a new filing, or sit under another registrant (ExxonMobil). Without this, LTM failed
  and XOM's "latest" grade rested on one factor of six.

### D25. Published metrics contract
- **Decision:** contracts.py (Pydantic) defines metrics.json. Metrics are keyed "<metric_id>:<period>" to
  match memo placeholders; every metric carries its XBRL inputs; an assumed-zero value is exported as status
  ok with a note; the checklist groups repeated log entries into one item naming the periods.
- **Why:** one source of truth for the site and the memo; every number traceable from the JSON alone.

### D26. Golden-set sheets
- **Decision:** generated blank from the latest 10-K, never overwritten once they exist; a finance-lease row
  (D18) and derived formulas identical to the engine's definitions.
- **Why:** the author's values must be independent of the tool's, and both must measure the same thing.

### D27. Chain revision 3: finance-lease current portion optional (approved 17 November 2026)
- **Decision:** in the finance-lease sum, FinanceLeaseLiabilityCurrent is optional (assumed zero, logged).
- **Why:** Caesars tags about $13.1bn of non-current finance-lease liabilities with no current-portion tag,
  so they were left out of its debt while their interest was in its interest expense. Tested on all 15
  companies before approval: only Caesars changes (LTM debt $11,558m -> $24,746m; debt / EBITDA 3.6x ->
  7.7x; SB-4 -> SB-5). Chain changes do not touch the frozen grid (grid-v1).

### D28. Text extraction with the standard-library HTML parser (phase 3)
- **Why:** about 60 readable lines, no dependency, 0.1 s per filing; handles inline XBRL by skipping the
  hidden header and display:none elements.
- **Rejected:** BeautifulSoup/lxml (more dependencies for no gain here); an LLM (cost, variance, untestable).

### D29. Rule-based section detection, every rule tied to a real filing
- **Decision:** headings only; titled beats bare; most text before a different item; 10-Q part from title;
  debt note by numbered heading with a debt title, ending at the next note number, searched across the
  document outside narrative sections; joint filers' statement items labelled from their titles.
- **Why:** deterministic and testable; the section-coverage report over all 15 companies drove each rule.
  Where rules fail, text stays unlabelled rather than guessed.

### D30. BM25 index as one JSON file per company in data/index/, committed
- **Decision:** passages, statistics and inverted index in one file (about 21 MB for 15 companies);
  deterministic bytes; the loader imports neither the EDGAR client nor pandas.
- **Why:** the live API (phase 7) needs the index at run time with no network and no state between
  requests. data/index/ is not in the plan's layout; it is separate from data/published/ because the site's
  pages never load it.
- **Rejected:** building the index at request time (slow, needs EDGAR); a database (none needed).

### D31. Saved filing texts as test fixtures
- **Decision:** three extracted texts (WMT 10-K, GT 10-K, VZ 10-Q), gzipped, with their source URLs.
- **Why:** section tests run against real filings without network access; gzip keeps them to 280 KB.

### D32. Chat Completions API, although Sail now labels its Responses API "recommended" (phase 4)
- **Why:** the plan fixed Chat Completions; Sail still lists it as stable, and it supports everything
  needed (json_schema structured output, strict function tools, service tier, reasoning effort). Re-read
  17 November 2026: `max_completion_tokens` is the output limit (`max_tokens` is rejected); `seed`, `stop`
  and `logprobs` are unsupported, so run-to-run spread is measured instead.
- **Rejected for now:** switching to the Responses API (no capability the project needs; one more change).

### D33. Idempotent retries; the OpenAI SDK's own retries switched off
- **Why:** Sail's retry guidance (re-read 17 November 2026) says only 429s and capacity 503s are refused
  before work starts; other errors may have started a generation, so a blind retry can pay twice. Every
  call sends an Idempotency-Key and reuses it on each retry (backoff: Retry-After, else 1, 2, 4 s + jitter;
  at most 4 attempts).

### D34. Tools and the answer format go in separate requests (approved 17 November 2026)
- **Decision:** the follow-up endpoint (phase 7) runs its lookup turns with tools only, then asks for the
  structured answer in a separate request with the response schema and no tools.
- **Why:** the capability probe (docs/sail-capability-probe.md, run twice) found GLM-5.3 and
  DeepSeek-V4-Pro skip the tool and invent a number when tools and a response schema share a request;
  DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash does not. The separated pattern passed for all three. Memo drafting and judging use
  structured output only, which all three pass.
- **Rejected:** dropping the two models (loses the cost-against-accuracy comparison); trusting combined
  requests (they produced fabricated numbers).

### D35. One reasoning-effort setting per role, the same for every model
- **Decision:** writer "medium", judge "low" (config/models.yaml); GLM-5.3 rejects "none".
- **Why:** comparable settings make the model comparison fair; the judge's task is narrow.

### D36. The judge also sees the engine values behind a claim's placeholders
- **Why:** a claim such as "leverage rose to {{m:...}}" has no passage to cite; giving the judge the
  values lets it catch a wrong direction or comparison. Passages are still the evidence for everything else.

### D37. A memo embeds only what it uses
- **Decision:** memo.json holds the metrics its claims, ladder and scorecard reference, and the passages its
  claims cite, so it is a self-contained dated snapshot; the full metric set stays in metrics.json.

### D38. Every model request and response is saved (data/runs/<TICKER>/<run>.jsonl)
- **Why:** results can be recomputed and audited without new model calls (PLAN.md 4.11); the API key is
  never in the request body, and a test checks the saved file does not contain it.

### D39. Judge evidence carries period dates; rating-rationale claims are judged against the scorecard
- **Why:** the first Walmart memo (run WMT-20261118, GLM-5.3) had true claims marked "partially supported"
  only because the judge saw "Revenue, FY-2" without the date it stands for, and a false rationale claim
  (that the grade was provisional) passed as "partially supported" because the judge never saw the
  scorecard. The writer is now told explicitly whether the grade is provisional.
- **Effect:** the first run's outputs are kept in data/runs/ for comparison; memos are regenerated.

### D40. Evaluation runs are resumable and recomputable (phase 5)
- **Decision:** eval memos go to evals/results/memos/<writer>/run<n>/ and are skipped if present; the report
  reads only saved files; judge candidates and seeded errors replay the saved drafts.
- **Why:** an interrupted run never pays twice, and every number can be recomputed without new model calls.

### D41. Golden sheets get a quote column for the fact questions (phase 5)
- **Why:** retrieval recall needs to know which passage the author located; a page number cannot be matched
  to a passage, a short copied quote can. The sheets were regenerated before the author had edited them.

### D42. Agency ratings: one rank per company, averaged across the agencies entered
- **Why:** the author may enter one, two or three agencies; averaging their positions on one scale (AAA/Aaa
  = 1 ... D/C = 22) keeps every company in the comparison. IG = BBB-/Baa3 or better.

### D43. Writer output limit raised from 8,000 to 16,000 tokens (approved 18 November 2026)
- **Why:** in the first golden runs DeepSeek-V4-Pro's reasoning (medium effort) used the whole 8,000-token
  limit in 11 draft calls (finish_reason "length", empty or cut-off answers), forcing repairs and leaving one
  memo section without a draft; GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash never reached it. The limit was measuring my
  setting, not the model. The same limit applies to every writer.
- **Effect:** DeepSeek-V4-Pro's five golden run-1 memos were regenerated; the capped versions are kept in
  evals/results/superseded/ with their raw outputs in data/runs/. GLM-5.3 and Flash memos are unaffected.

### D44. The watchlist job triggers a Vercel deploy hook after committing (phase 6)
- **Why:** Vercel's docs (troubleshoot-project-collaboration, last updated 13 March 2026; KB guide, 16 October
  2026) say a Hobby team deploys only commits whose author is the team owner, so the job's bot commits would not
  deploy. A deploy hook (a secret URL, stored as a GitHub secret; Hobby allows 5 per project, 60 calls an hour)
  starts the deploy instead. To be confirmed once the repository and project exist.
- **Rejected:** authoring bot commits as the owner (blurs who changed what); Vercel Cron (cannot write files).

### D45. Staleness is an event, not a comparison
- **Decision:** the job marks a memo stale when it sees a new filing; regenerating the memo marks it current.
- **Why:** simple to explain and to test, and it matches the review step: a stale memo stays stale until a
  human has regenerated and reviewed it.

### D46. Published memos come from the GLM-5.3 evaluation run until the models are chosen
- **Why:** they are already verified, so publishing them costs nothing; once the author chooses the writer and
  judge, build-all regenerates (or copies the chosen writer's run and re-judges it) in one command.

### D47. Deploy layout: one Python function for /api, the Vite build as static files (phase 7)
- **Decision:** `api/index.py` exposes the FastAPI app; `vercel.json` rewrites `/api/*` to it, builds `web/`
  and serves `web/dist` (with the published JSON copied to `dist/data`). The function may run 75 seconds, so the
  app's own 60-second limit answers first with a plain 503.
- **Why:** Vercel's docs, re-read 18 November 2026, still detect FastAPI from an `app` object in a standard
  entry file (app.py, index.py, server.py, main.py at the root, in src/ or app/, or `tool.vercel.entrypoint`)
  and recommend a newer "Services" setup for a frontend plus backend, without saying whether Hobby has it. The
  plan's default layout uses only long-standing features. Unverified until a preview deploy (needs approval).
- **Rejected:** Services (Hobby availability unknown); a FastAPI app at the root (Vercel would treat the whole
  project as a Python app).

### D48. A live answer keeps only claims the judge marks supported
- **Decision:** `/api/ask` runs the memo's checks on every claim and keeps only "supported"; partly supported
  and unsupported claims go to the "removed" list with the reason.
- **Why:** a memo is reviewed by a person before publication and its partly supported claims are marked and
  listed; a live answer is read straight away with no reviewer, so the bar is higher.

### D49. Follow-up limits sized for 60 seconds
- **Decision:** at most 3 lookup rounds, 3 lookups per round, 5 passages per search, 5 claims; writer reasoning
  effort low with a 4,000-token cap; judges run in parallel; each model request times out at 45 seconds with
  one retry. The final answer always comes from a schema-only request, even when the model stops looking
  things up early (D34 applied strictly).
- **Evidence:** a two-round Walmart question took 18.3 s and an out-of-scope one 2.5 s (GLM-5.3, 18 November
  2026, one run each, so indicative only).

### D50. The data contract is exported as one JSON Schema; TypeScript types are generated from it
- **Decision:** `pipeline/export_schema.py` writes `web/src/contracts/schema.json` from the Pydantic models
  (published files in serialization mode, with defaulted fields marked required because they are always
  written; the request body in validation mode); `json-schema-to-typescript` generates `types.ts`. Tests fail if
  either is out of date, and every published file is validated against its model.
- **Why:** contracts.py stays the single source of the shapes, and a contract change cannot silently break the
  interface.

### D51. The interface formats numbers exactly as the Python engine does
- **Decision:** `web/src/format.ts` mirrors `format_metric`, rounding like Python (the double's exact value,
  ties to even); a test compares it with every metric chip in the 15 published memos.
- **Why:** the first version used JavaScript's `toFixed`, and the test caught HCA's FY0 debt ($47.25 billion)
  reading "$47.3 billion" in a table and "$47.2 billion" in the memo.
- **Rejected:** publishing a display string for every value (a contract change; can be proposed for phase 9).

### D52. Plain React with hash routing; the npm lockfile is generated with npm 12.2.1
- **Decision:** no router or component library (phase 9 replaces the look); routes are URL hashes, so the static
  host needs no rewrite rules. Exact versions, each at least two weeks old on 18 November 2026. The lockfile was
  generated with npm 12.2.1 via npx because the installed npm 10.9.3 crashes on this dependency set (an internal
  error in its peer-dependency resolver); installs use `npm ci`, which reads the lockfile and works on npm 10.

### D53. Strategy artifacts are rendered from templates, like the memos (phase 8)
- **Decision:** artifacts 1 to 5 are templates in docs/strategy/templates/ whose figures are placeholders filled
  from evals/results/results.json and evals/timings.csv; a test fails if any other digit appears (identifiers
  and list numbering aside). The decision log stays hand-written. The method page is generated from
  config/grid.yaml and the engine's formula strings. All of it is published as about.json.
- **Why:** the plan requires that every number in an artifact matches a results file or the timing log; making
  it impossible to type one is stronger than checking afterwards, and a re-run of the evaluation updates the
  documents with one command.
- **Rejected:** hand-written artifacts checked by a search for matching numbers (a typed number that happens to
  match a result would pass).

### D54. Opportunity-map ratings are words, and the model choice waits for the labels
- **Decision:** the map rates value, feasibility and risk as High, Medium or Low, labelled as the author's
  judgment for review. The model memo states a rule for choosing, written before the labels exist, instead of
  a choice.
- **Why:** numeric scores would look like measurements; and choosing a model before the human labels exist
  would rest on the provisional judge grading its own writing.

### D55. The control table cites the 2026 guidance only for vocabulary
- **Decision:** the risk and control table states the guidance's scope (its definition of a model, footnote 3,
  the $30 billion relevance line, no enforceable standards) before the table, and maps each control to a
  borrowed term; it claims no compliance.
- **Why:** read from the primary documents on 18 November 2026. The ratio engine is outside the definition and
  the generative parts are outside the scope, so a compliance claim would be false; the vocabulary is still how a
  bank's model-risk team would assess the tool.

documents.title: Method
documents.markdown:
# Method

Every figure is computed by code from the company's XBRL data in its 10-K and 10-Q filings, using the
most recently filed value for each period. LTM (last twelve months) adds the latest year-to-date flows to
the last fiscal year and subtracts the prior year's year-to-date flows. A figure that cannot be found is
shown as "not available"; it is never estimated.

## Ratios

| Ratio | Definition |
|---|---|
| EBITDA | `operating_income + d_and_a` |
| Debt / EBITDA | `total_debt / EBITDA` |
| Net leverage | `(total_debt - cash - short_term_investments) / EBITDA` |
| EBITDA / interest | `EBITDA / interest_expense` |
| FCF / debt | `(cfo - capex) / total_debt` |
| Liquidity coverage | `(cash + short_term_investments + undrawn_revolver + max(cfo, 0)) / (short_term_debt + capex + dividends)` |
| Near-term maturity cover | `(short_term_debt + maturity_year_2) / (cash + short_term_investments + undrawn_revolver)` |

## The SB scorecard (grid-v1)

SB grades are a student's stylized scorecard, not credit ratings. Each factor is placed in a band from 1
(strongest) to 6 (weakest); the grade comes from the weighted average band. A value exactly on a threshold gets the weaker band (tie rule "worse").

| Factor | Weight | Band 1 | Band 2 | Band 3 | Band 4 | Band 5 | Band 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Debt / EBITDA | 20% | under 1x | 1x to under 2x | 2x to under 3x | 3x to under 4.5x | 4.5x to under 6.5x | 6.5x or more |
| Net debt / EBITDA | 10% | under 0.5x | 0.5x to under 1.5x | 1.5x to under 2.5x | 2.5x to under 4x | 4x to under 6x | 6x or more |
| EBITDA / interest | 25% | over 15x | over 10x to 15x | over 6x to 10x | over 3.5x to 6x | over 2x to 3.5x | 2x or less |
| FCF / debt | 20% | over 40% | over 25% to 40% | over 15% to 25% | over 8% to 15% | over 0% to 8% | 0% or less |
| Liquidity sources / uses | 15% | over 2.5x | over 2x to 2.5x | over 1.5x to 2x | over 1.2x to 1.5x | over 1x to 1.2x | 1x or less |
| Debt due in 24 months / (cash + undrawn revolver) | 10% | under 0.25x | 0.25x to under 0.5x | 0.5x to under 0.75x | 0.75x to under 1x | 1x to under 1.5x | 1.5x or more |

Special cases: net cash scores band 1; a company with no debt scores band 1 on the debt factors; a ratio that cannot be computed meaningfully scores a fixed band when the reason is EBITDA at or below zero (band 6); no debt (band 1); no uses of cash (band 1); no cash or undrawn revolver (band 6). Any other unscorable factor is left out.

| Weighted score | Grade |
|---|---|
| up to 1.5 | SB-1 |
| over 1.5 to 2.5 | SB-2 |
| over 2.5 to 3.5 | SB-3 |
| over 3.5 to 4.5 | SB-4 |
| over 4.5 to 5.5 | SB-5 |
| over 5.5 | SB-6 |

A weighted score of 3.5 or less counts as "IG-like" (investment-grade-like) in the comparison with agency ratings. When a factor cannot be scored, the remaining weights are scaled up and the grade is marked provisional.

documents.title: Known risks and limitations
documents.markdown:
# Known risks and limitations

Seeded from PLAN.md section 4.15; later items were added while building, with the phase that added them.

## Seeded from the plan

- XBRL tagging varies by company and over time; extension tags are invisible to the API; LongTermDebt is
  ambiguous; restatements change history; mergers break trends. Handling is in PLAN.md 4.5.
- No business-risk factors (scale, diversification, cyclicality) in the scorecard, so it will misjudge
  some companies against agencies.
- Section parsing of filing HTML can fail; tables are flattened to text.
- Keyword retrieval misses paraphrases.
- A quoted figure can match a number in the passage that refers to something else; the judge is the only
  check on that.
- The judge can be wrong, and when the judge and writer are the same model it may be lenient. Human labels
  on the golden set are the reference.
- Model outputs vary between runs; Sail may retire a model.
- The scheduled job may be disabled by GitHub after long inactivity; deploys from bot commits are
  unverified.
- The rate limit is per IP only; the spend backstop is a small prepaid Sail balance with auto-recharge off.
- Agency ratings carry redistribution terms. By default the site shows only aggregate agreement; ask
  before showing per-company ratings.

## Added in phase 1

- Chain revision 1 (decision D18) resolved the phase-1 chain issues. Remaining risks:
  - Rank 1 total debt adds finance-lease liabilities from their own tags. If a company's
    LongTermDebtNoncurrent line already includes finance leases and it also tags FinanceLeaseLiability in
    its lease note, leases are counted twice. The reconciliation check catches this only when another
    candidate is reported for the same date.
  - Rank 2 pairs a combined debt-and-lease tag with short-term debt. If short-term debt comes from
    LongTermDebtCurrent alone, the current portion of finance leases may be missing (usually small).
  - At 30 September 2026 Verizon tags its whole "debt maturing within one year" line as LongTermDebtCurrent,
    so its short-term borrowings are logged as "assumed zero" although they sit inside that figure; the
    total is right.
  - DebtLongtermAndShorttermCombinedAmount (now rank 5) varies in scope by company. Walmart's
    reconciliation warns against it in every period; that is expected and stays visible.
- The derived operating income (pre-tax income plus interest expense) includes non-operating items such as
  other income and expense, so it differs from a true operating line.
- InterestExpense and InterestExpenseNonoperating are assumed to include finance-lease interest; this is
  not checked company by company.
- Exact date matching means a fact with irregular dates is reported as not available rather than matched.
- Test fixtures are trimmed (chain tags only, periods from 2021) to keep the repository small; the full
  responses are re-creatable from EDGAR.

## Added in phase 2

- Undrawn revolver capacity is tagged only by Verizon among the 15. For the others it counts as zero
  (logged), which understates liquidity coverage and overstates near-term maturity cover, pushing those two
  factors towards weaker bands (e.g. Walmart).
- Maturity tables use company extension tags for some buckets, invisible to the API: Kohl's (all buckets),
  HCA, Goodyear, Procter & Gamble and ExxonMobil ("after year 5"). Their ladder totals and the ladder
  reconciliation are not available; Kohl's near-term maturity cover is not scored, so its grade is
  provisional.
- Caesars tags about $13.1bn of lease obligations as non-current finance-lease liabilities without a
  current-portion tag. Since chain revision 3 (D27) they count as debt; what they are (the counterparties)
  is to be confirmed in its 10-K.
- Net interest understates gross interest expense where interest income is material.
- ExxonMobil's latest figures (31 March 2026) are about six months older than most companies'.
- The scorecard is ratio-only: no business-risk factors and no operating-lease adjustment, so companies with
  large operating leases (such as retailers) can look stronger than under methods that adjust for leases.
  This is by design, and the comparison with agency ratings will measure its effect.
- Several reconciliation warnings (total debt against alternative candidates, ladder against total debt)
  remain open for a reviewer to resolve; none changes a value.

## Added in phase 3

- Section detection gaps (reports/section-coverage.md): ExxonMobil's 10-K uses a cross-reference format
  (Item 7 and Item 8 point to a later "Financial Section"), so its MD&A is not labelled; HCA's and Oracle's
  Item 8 is a one-line pointer and their statements sit at the end of the document, after the last Item, so
  they are labelled "other_item" (their debt notes are still found); some
  10-Qs have no separate debt note (Procter & Gamble, Oracle, ExxonMobil) and P&G's 10-Q has no liquidity
  heading in the list.
- Tables are flattened to text; in some filings each table cell becomes its own line, which makes passages
  of bare numbers.
- 10-Qs repeat much of the previous quarter's text, so near-identical passages appear from several
  filings; de-duplication happens when passages are merged for the memo (phase 4).
- Keyword search misses paraphrases; recall is measured in phase 5.
- Facts that appear only in text (e.g. Walmart's $15.0bn of undrawn committed credit lines) are not used by
  the ratio engine, which reads XBRL only.

## Added in phase 4

- A quoted figure passes the number check if the same number appears anywhere in the cited passage, even
  with a different meaning; the judge is the only check on that (as the plan anticipated).
- GLM-5.3 is both the default writer and the provisional judge, so the judge may be lenient on its own
  writing; phase 5 calibrates the judge against human labels.
- Model outputs vary between runs and cannot be pinned (no seed); phase 5 measures the spread.
- GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro invent values when tools and a response schema share a request (probe); the
  design avoids that pattern.

## Added in phase 6

- Liquidity and near-term-maturity flags are noisy: 14 of 15 companies do not tag undrawn revolver capacity,
  which counts as zero, so most companies carry one of these flags (e.g. Walmart, with $15bn of undrawn lines
  in its 10-Q text).
- Vercel Hobby deploys only commits authored by the account owner (Vercel docs, last updated March and
  October 2026), so the watchlist's bot commits rely on a deploy hook; not verified until a repository and
  Vercel project exist.
- ExxonMobil is refreshed on every run (its newest 10-Q's facts sit under its new registrant); this costs one
  extra EDGAR request a day and changes no file.
- The scheduled run is off until the author approves it (phase 10).

## Added in phase 7

- `/api/ask` has no rate limit or login until the Vercel Firewall rule is added (phase 10); until then anyone
  with the URL could spend Sail credit.
- When an answer passes the 60-second limit the caller gets a 503, but model requests already started run on
  (up to 45 seconds each) and are billed.
- The follow-up judge is the provisional judge (GLM-5.3), the same model as the provisional writer.
- The maturity ladder is as of the last 10-K. Its first bucket keeps the XBRL tag's wording, "debt maturing in
  the next twelve months", meaning the twelve months after that fiscal year-end; an answer can read it as twelve
  months from today, and the judge accepted that reading in the smoke test (Walmart, maturity_year_1:FY0).
- Not verified until a preview deploy: whether Vercel's Python runtime installs from pyproject.toml without
  the dev group, whether the rewrite keeps the /api/... path FastAPI routes on, and whether the 21 MB search
  index is bundled with the function.
- Placeholder interface: plain styling; trends and the maturity ladder are tables, not charts; the watchlist
  screen lacks the design brief's "change in leverage and coverage since the prior year-end" column, which
  watchlist.json does not carry; the results screen reads evals.json's untyped `results` defensively.
- Checklist sign-off lives in one browser's localStorage: it is not an audit trail.

## Added in phase 8

- The opportunity map's ratings are the author's judgment (drafted for review), not measurements.
- The effort comparison is pending until the author records timings; when recorded, it describes one analyst

- The model recommendation is provisional until the claim labels and judge calibration exist.
